units.text: A migration and a modernization are two different milestones. After the rehost, measure actual cost, latency, and application behavior. That tells you where later changes could pay off rather than treating every component as a redesign candidate.

Right-size and harden what you have first. Then choose a high-value capability to migrate to a managed service. Compare its behavior and operating effort before taking the same step for other components.

Follow a migration request from source identity to A W S. Map roles with least privilege and use encrypted transport appropriate to the path. Private routing is not proof the data is encrypted, and encryption does not replace authorization.

At the destination, verify access scope, key permissions, secret management, and audit evidence. Check that storage and logs meet residency requirements, and that an authorized restore succeeds without exposing the migrated data.

Moving a whole server, synchronizing database rows, and converting schema are different jobs. Use M G N for supported server rehosting, D M S for supported data movement, and schema conversion when the destination engine differs. Separate migration tasks can work together.

If the application stays the same and you need to move files, compare a transfer service such as DataSync. If the runtime or capability itself must change, a replatform or refactor is the design choice, not a file-copy tool.

A wave is not ready merely because the date is on the calendar. Confirm owners, dependency paths, access, monitoring, and recovery readiness. Identify the actual signal that would stop the cutover before customers are affected.

After the move, use agreed acceptance evidence: representative transactions, dependency reachability, healthy telemetry, and an owner able to operate the workload. If a required check fails, follow the fallback decision. Decommission only after stabilization.

What exactly stopped working? A single component failure may leave the application running, while losing a Region or access to an account can take out otherwise healthy resources. Corrupt data is another boundary: a running replica may faithfully copy the damage.

Estimate the allowable interruption and data loss with the owner before choosing technology. Test the particular failure your plan is meant to survive. A successful instance failover is not evidence of recovery from an account loss.

The outage starts both comparisons. Look backward to the recovered data point for actual data loss. Look forward to the time the service is usable again for actual downtime. A booted server does not stop the second clock if the application cannot yet serve real requests.

Measure a known committed record and run a representative read or write after restoration. Compare those observations with the objectives instead of treating the backup timestamp or a green health check as proof.

Backup and restore leaves more work to do during an incident. Pilot light keeps the data core ready, but still needs the rest of the serving environment brought up. Choose based on what your recovery window allows.

A warm standby can already serve at a reduced scale. An active-active deployment already serves from multiple sites, but data and routing decisions become harder. Treat the times in a comparison as relative expectations, not service guarantees.

A backup copy preserves data, not every part of a runnable application. Keep infrastructure definitions, tested images, required configuration, and a secure way to recover secrets and key access. Place supported recovery copies where the intended failure cannot remove them together.

Restore data into the recovery environment and deploy the application against it. Prove that a client can complete a transaction before shifting production traffic. This rebuild time is the trade-off of keeping less running between incidents.

Pilot light keeps a small data core and supporting services alive; it is not a full-scale serving environment. Before trouble, verify replication, launch templates, permissions, and quotas. Data is not useful if the missing application tier cannot be started in time.

During recovery, activate or scale the application tier, verify current data and application health, then redirect traffic. This step is what separates pilot light from a standby already able to handle traffic.

Warm standby runs the full application in the recovery Region, but at reduced capacity. A health check there can prove the minimum path works; it does not prove the fleet can handle all production demand.

Scale the standby, confirm dependencies and data are ready, and redirect traffic according to the runbook. Test sustained workload at the target level, and record whether the whole operation meets the recovery target.

Both Regions can handle app traffic without both Aurora clusters accepting local writes. Follow the replication arrow: writes commit on the primary, and Aurora replicates the result to the secondary. If supported write forwarding is enabled there, it sends statements back to the primary; that is a different path from replication.

Choose how to route traffic and define who owns writes before a failure. A different data store that genuinely accepts writes in both Regions also needs explicit consistency and conflict rules. Decide how to restore your preferred state, and test that procedure separately.

Protect a source server by continuously copying its disk changes to a low-cost staging area. Elastic Disaster Recovery can then launch recovery instances as needed. That lets you keep replicas ready without keeping a full-size recovery application running all the time.

Choose an appropriate point, launch recovery instances, and verify the actual workload before moving users. A drill practices recovery; failback is a separate controlled movement, not an automatic reversal of production traffic.

In this drill, source servers continue serving while replicated disks feed a recovery instance. Check replication status first, then launch a non-disruptive drill and verify connectivity, files, and service behavior without changing live D N S.

After a real failover, writes may exist only on the recovery side. Replicate and validate those changes before returning traffic to the original environment. A successful drill helps test the sequence without treating it as a real failback.

A successful backup job means the copy was created, not that your workload can run from it. Choose a recovery point and restore it in a separate test environment so the original workload stays untouched.

Run integrity checks and a real application transaction. Record both the date of the newest recovered data and the time the service became usable. Those are the observations that tell you whether the backup plan met its objectives.

Define common backup rules centrally and assign them through A W S Organizations. Member accounts still need supported resources, protected plans and vaults, and the permissions for any cross-account copies. A policy assignment is not evidence that a given resource was backed up.

Check backup reports, copy results, and restore-test evidence. Use audit controls to surface missing coverage. Confirm that the destination vault has a usable recovery point for the specific workload you intend to recover.

Backup frequency determines the spacing of potential recovery points. Retention tells you how long to keep them. Decide each separately: a small recovery-point objective does not imply every hourly copy must be retained for years.

When the backup resource type supports a cold-storage transition, use the A W S Backup lifecycle and account for restore behavior. This is not a universal move through regular S three storage classes. Choose legal hold or immutable retention separately from tiering when protection requires it.

Match the control to what is protected: S three Object Lock for object versions, E B S snapshot lock for snapshots, and A W S Backup Vault Lock for recovery points in a backup vault. Governance and compliance have different authority and retention rules. Choose and review the mode before committing.

Retention protects the recovery point from premature change or deletion under the configured mode; it does not prove the recovery team can read it. Test an authorized restore with the expected permissions and keys.
